uncited: Object Decomposition and Composition refers to a family of NeRF architectures that explicitly separate a scene into distinct semantic or geometric entities (objects) to enable instance-level editing, manipulation, and analysis.
Unlike standard NeRFs that treat the scene as a monolithic volume, these methods introduce mechanisms to identify, isolate, and recombine individual objects.

This family is distinguished from siblings like [Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations](12495-signed-distance-function-sdf-representations.md) by its focus on semantic/instance separation rather than just boundary representation, and from [Mixture-of-Experts and Modular Architectures](14429-mixture-of-experts-and-modular-architectures.md) by its specific goal of compositional scene editing rather than just computational efficiency.

The core task of a NeRF network architecture is to learn a continuous volumetric scene representation $F_\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c})$, where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the spatial position, $\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the viewing direction, $\sigma$ is the volume density, and $\mathbf{c}$ is the view-dependent color.
The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations.
The concept of decomposing scenes into compositional parts emerged early in NeRF research.
These works laid the groundwork for later methods that integrate decomposition directly into the optimization loop for editing.
